I do not think all the paragraphs have been read. With reference to paragraph (e) of section 6, dealing with an alien female infant who has been granted entry for a homestead, and who is prevented from becoming a British subject by the provisions of the Naturalization Act of 1914, I would like the minister to give me a concrete example of such a case."

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Take, for instance, the case of a woman who complies with the conditions enabling her to get entry and who marries an alien. She is not empowered under the provisions of the Naturalization Act to naturalize, consequently she could not qualify to get her patent at all unless this provision was inserted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7-Area of cultivation may be reduced.

Under the old Act the power to state the area of cultivation required was a matter for the Governor in Council, whilst this amendment brings it directly under the jurisdiction of the minister. Is there any particular reason why the change should be made?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Linder the former law, in case of pre-emption as distinguished from cases of homesteads, the whole township had to be declared of the character set out here in order to enable any pre-emptor to have his cultivation reduced. In that case, one-half of the township might be incapable of having the requisite duties performed on any quarter-section, and the other half might be just the other way. Indeed, you might have a case in which the law could be applied to one-half of the section and not to the other half. The first object of this amendment, there-



fore, is to permit a distinction between one pre-emption and another pre-emption, not between one township and another township. That being the case, it becomes desirable that the necessity for an Order in Council should be dispensed with. The recommendations are made on the report of the homestead inspector in each case, and I do not see any value in the intervention of the Governor in Council. In other instances also the necessity for Order in Council is being dispensed with. The time of Council has been taken up with the reading of Orders in which members of Council do not take any interest, and which of necessity must be a matter of administration, to be left to the responsible minister.
In the official Gazette I often see recommendations by the minister to extend the time of a man's residence on a homestead and the like.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be in the case of a homesteader. The Order in Council would set out that that particular homesteader was relieved of his duty, but in the case of a pre-emptor the power was given to place townships, not single preemptions, in that category.

The publishing of those Orders in Council in the Gazette must serve as an official report available to the public, and also as a precedent in the case of further applications of a like nature being made. Unless there is some objection other than that of taking Council's time in reading the recommendations, I do not see why this change should be made. Otherwise, there is no way of ascertaining what changes are made or what conditions are required by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The regulations are
known to homesteaders who can easily secure copies of them, and who therefore 'know the conditions under which their cultivation duties may be reduced. I do not think the public generally are sufficiently interested in whether a certain homesteader has his ploughing duties reduced from thirty to twenty acres to warrant the publication of each Order in Council in the Gazette.
But the settler is.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The settler is, but he knows it without reading the Gazette. I doubt if there is one settler in the whole West who takes the official Gazette.

If some one made an application to my bon. friend in the course

of his practice of law with regard to the reduction of cultivation duties, my horn, friend would probably refer to the Gazette.
Mr. IA1EIGHEN: If il were the practising lawyer 'I would go to the regulations and there find; the conditions under which my client was entitled to apply for a reduction of cultivation duties. The reduction would then be made, and my client would have .a letter from the department, stating that his area bad been reduced. That is all the authority he needs; I do not think that either the laywer or the entrant would look at the official Gazette.

No, but there should be
a general rule.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The only rule you can
have is in the regulations. One man might have a homestead in which thirty acres would be required; another right across the road might have a homestead where eighteen acres would be required, and some one else to the north might have one where twenty-five would be required-all depending on the varying character of the soil.
It is concentrating everything in the minister's hands.

I suggest to the minister
that he incorporate in this provision some discretionary power to reduce the area of cultivation where land becomes flooded, and it is impossible to get under cultivation the number of acres required by the Act.	i

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I see no objection to inserting the word "flooded" after the words "wooded, rocky."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 8-holder may obtain patent by extra payments where he is in default for residence duties solely:
Mr. A1EIGHEN: Under the law as it stands now and has stood for about three years the pre-emptor who has obtained patents for his homestead and is in residence on either his homestead or his pre-emption may, if he has done his cultivation duties and effected the necessary improvements, secure his patent by simply paying up. Previous to three years ago that was not the case; the pre-emptor had to complete his - residence duties as well in respect of preemption, and might complete them on the homestead. This rule was relaxed three years ago to the extent of enabling him, if he continued in residence after he was through wdth his homestead duties and had

his patents, to dispense with all the other residence duties by simply paying up. Cases, however, arose where the homesteader who had pre-empted left his homestead, forsook his residence duties altogether, came back and reinstated himself as a resident on the homestead, and then demanded his patent on the payment of $3 an acre. Cases of hardship arose where the department had to require such a man to perform his three years' residence duties. This provision, therefore, is to enable the department to give him this answer: you have abandoned1 your residence duties; if you do not want to go ahead and perform them you must pay $3 an acre extra for the land. There are cases where men who are in business want to avoid the necessity of the residence duties, and where it is felt that it would be equitable to allow them to do so on paying that extra price for the land.
Section agreed to.
On section 9-certificate of recommendation to holder of entry for a pre-emption on completing all duties except payment:
Do I understand that certificate to have the same value, so far as the rights of the entrant on the land are concerned, as if he had the patent? He can dispose of his interest?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

But 'before the patent is issued, the patentee, or whoever gets his interest in the land, has to pay the purchase price. What is the particular object of this? Has there 'been any hardship on the homesteader because he could not get the money?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Hon. members Who were in the last Parliament will remember that this subject was pressed upon the House by the hon. member who then represented Saskatoon. Very many cases arise where the holder of a pre-emption owes the preemption moneys to the Grown. He has performed his cultivation duty; he desires to raise a loan with which to pay off the Crown; but he cannot do so; he can do nothing at all with his land until he secures his patent. In order to meet difficulties of that kind in relation to homesteads, there previously was a provision in the law for granting certificates of recommendation for homesteads, but those were abolished in 1908. There was not the same reason for the certificate of recommendation for homesteads that there existed for certificates of recommendations for pre-emptions, because there could be no money owing to the Crown
m
in relation to homesteads, homesteads being free. But where a pre-emptor finds himself in the position that he wants to pay off the Crown, but there is no means by which he can put a loan on his pre-emption in order to pay off the Crown to get the patent, he is practically forbidden access to the money markets. This provision gives him that access for the period of a year, which period may be extended at the discretion of the minister. The effect is that he can deal with his homestead, as if he owned it, subject, of course, to the possibility of that certificate of recommendation failing unless lived up to within the year.

In a case like that, would the lender put his mortgage on record before the Crown was>
paid off? What would 'be the effect, supposing I advanced a man $1,000 upon a pre-emption and he gave -me a mortgage and I put my mortgage on record before the patent was issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The certificate itself sets out what he owes to the -Crown, and any rights -he has to mortgage or deal with his land are naturally subject to the indebtedness to the Crown.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Entry for purchased homesteads :
That is the same thing as for pre-emption. *

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The same thing in the case of a purchased homestead.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Myers moved to amend section 10 by adding the word " flooded " after the word " rocky ".

Might I point out that by adding the word " flooded " there, you make it possible of interpretation that the land must always be flooded? I would suggest it would be better to say " or subject to floods from time to time ". I believe that is the meaning of the amendment. I do not apprehend that, in order to have the benefits of this proviso, the land must always be flooded. I would imagine it would be subject to floods from time to time so that it could not be cultivated as fully as if it were not subject to floods.
-Sir SAM HUGHES: I think the point is very well taken. In the Northwest there are tens of thousands of acres of good land that are flooded at times. Such land could be made arable by drainage. Rocky land could not be made good by any process known to farmers. In my opinion the word

"flooded" should not he inserted at all. I can point out to the Minister of the Interior tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of acres of such land in the Northwest of Canada that in time will be the best land in the country, and all it wants is a little drainage. Although that land is flooded to-day, it should not be exempted.
Mr. MEIiGHEN:	The section as it has
been amended at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Myers) is the best possible for the following reason. It is not intended to exempt land that ie only subject to flooding, that may be all right one year and perhaps flooded another year, .because the homestead duties can be performed the second or third year. If you make it simply "subject to floods," then the door is opened too wide, because there is a great proportion of land, as the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) has said, that is subject to floods. But- take the case of land say adjoining lake Manitoba, which is near my own home. A man may homestead a quaTter-section there, and there may be only .a fraction of that quarter-section that is really capable of cultivation. Why? Because the rest is flooded :by the lake. It is not only subject to the floods, it is flooded land, and it is only right and proper that in a case of that kind his duties should be proportionately reduced. ,It has been the practice of the department so to reduce them. To put the word " flooded ", as suggested by the hon. member, covers a case of that sort. If you use the words "subject to floods," the door is opened too wide, and it would enable a reduction to be made, because merely in a certain year the land was covered by water, and in such a case the duties might be capable of being performed the next year.

As the minister is aware, two or three charges of dynamite properly placed might drain all the flooded land around lake Manitoba. I can point out one place in the Northwest, that I have had in view for a long time, that is flooded on account of a beaver meadow. We have not secured it yet, but we are watching for an opportunity to get hold of it. A week's digging will drain it. Although that land is flooded to-day, at an expenditure of less than fifty dollars it can be made arable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In a case of that kind it will be the duty of the minister to reduce the area of cultivation.
If he has the authority, that is all right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 12-sale of agricultural lands to entrant prevented from completing duties but with equitable claim:
Is not that provided in the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section is the same as the old Act except that the power is placed in the hands of the minister, instead of in the Governor in Council. My hon. friend will agree that any man wlic has had the training of a Solicitor Genera! can he trusted with that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-sale or lease of lands unsuitable for cultivation:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This section is important in this sense: it gives the department the same power to deal with lands that should be reclaimed by drainage that it now has with regard to lands that should be reclaimed by irrigation. Section 34, if this amendment is agreed to, will read:
Lands unsuitable for cultivation without the aid of irrigation or drainage, or lands required in connection with any system of irrigation or drainage may be sold or leased in such manner and under such terms and conditions as are fixed by the Governor in Council subject to the provisions of the Irrigation Act.
In November, 1916, conferences were held between representatives of the Governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and representatives of the Irrigation Branch of the Interior Department, at which arrangements were arrived at drawing the line of responsibility with regard to irrigation and drainage as between the provinces and the Dominion. These arrangements were afterwards implemented by legislation in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I think also in Manitoba, hut at all events, in the other two provinces. A scheme was also devised at the conference whereby the provinces might enter upon irrigation and drainage enterprises affecting Dominion lands, and the responsibility of the Dominion with regard to those enterprises was defined. Therefore, it is now the part of wisdom to place the drainage lands of the Crown in the same position as the irrigation lands, so we can deal with them as we are now able to deal with the irrigated lands.
Has there ever been any arrangement between the provinces and the Dominion with regard to what are known as the marsh lands, or has there ever been any transfer of these lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend refers to the swamp lands?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Those lands have been transferred from the province of Manitoba to the Crown; there were none in the other provinces.
It would be to lands of that sort this Act would apply in the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; such of those
swamp lands as are unsuitable for cultivation without the aid of drainage. Portions of those lands may not need drainage at all, even though described as swamp lands.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-Regulations to control disposal of timber and pulpwood berths:
Mr- LEMIEUX: These lands are disposed of by public tender?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. The object of this section is to enable the Governor in Council to extend the area in the case of pulpwood leases. Of course, a pulpmill will not be established on the basis of an area that is insufficient for its requirements for any reasonable length of time.
The object is to increase the area in the case of pulpwood?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I am not familiar with the original law, but paragraph (c) of this Bill says: "no offer by tender shall be accepted unless accompanied by the full amount of the bonus." I suppose bonus and bid mean the same?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, in -a sense. Tenderers have to agree to pay the license fee, Which is fixed. Then in addition to that they give a bonus, which really means a bid.
Mr. MoMIASTER: It does not mean they will have to accompany their bid with the full purchase price?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: With the full purchase price except the license fee, which is based on the amount of timber cut.

Might I suggest that
that might operate against the poorer tenderers, and perhaps result in the department's not getting as high a price as might otherwise be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has always been the
practice to collect the purchase price of the berth before the timber is cut. I think it would be rather the part of folly to wait until the timber was partially or wholly cut before collecting the purchase price of the berth. As soon as a man goes into one of these berths he immediately commences ito deplete the supply, and we collect as he proceeds to cut, the license being in proportion to the amount taken off.

I't has occurred to me that in the far Western Provinces through ladk of sufficient 'advertising and on account of the long distances, there might be a very limited number of tenderers, and as a result the pulpwood limits, which are very valuable to-day, might be sold for a song. What is tlhe policy of the department with regard to 'these sales? Is an outside price fixed after a preliminary cruise of the limits? I understand that in Quebec and Ontario the outside price is generally based on the report of the cruiser.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is the practice of the department and has been since 1908, to have a cruise of the area made by an inspector, and an upset price is fixed, based on his report.
By the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and sixty days' advertising in every case-a minimum of sixty days in one newspaper of local circulation, and in one newspaper of at least provincial circulation. All timber berths are sold by public auction, so that every possible chance to exploit the department, I think, is eliminated.	.
Does the minister state that it was the practice to have these limits cruised?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How long since?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Will the hon. minister explain the system of opening tenders in the department? In ancient days we have heard that there was a possibility of tenders not being properly looked after in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The system is to have no tenders. The sale is by public auction; consequently there are no tenders to open.
Where will the auction be held?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the office of the crown timber agent for the district.
Do I understand that when the limit is put up the bidders pay in cash so much per mile, which is called a bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So much for the entire berth. That is the bonus. Then, in addition to that, the bidder has to pay so much per thousand feet.
That is the stumpage?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Does he not pay a yearly license?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He pays five dollars per square mile in addition to that. There are other elements in the payment. There is the stumpage of fifty cents per thousand which he pays, then five dollars per square mile, and then the bonus.
The five dollars is for the license, and he pays the stumpage as he cuts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And an auction sale is held to ascertain what bonus is to be paid besides. The man paying the highest bonus gets the limit.

It appears to me that in many cases it may ,be a very great hardship to have to pay a bonus in a lump sum, especially in a case where, as often happens, timber being much more inaccessible now than in previous years, it is necessary, either to put in a railway or build flumes in order to get the logs out. This entails considerable expenditure of capital, and it might very well be that the bonus should extend over a number of years, instead of being paid1 in a lump sum. To my mind the license fee is too small, and it has given rise to this practice, in many cases, even after the timber berth has been logged off, the company holding it continues to hold it, and pays a small annual rental, which does not amount to anything, but the berth is a great asset to the company in making a statement on paper to the shareholders or the bank. They may have a good many square miles of holdings, but a large proportion of them may have been logged off, and yet on paper they have still very large holdings. In this way they are in a position to .show these berths as an asset in their statement to the shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The answer to the first inquiry is that the bonus does not require in certain cases to be all paid at once. The regulation reads:
6. Purchases to the amount of one thousand dollars or under shall he, paid in cash at the time of sale. Purchases over one thousand dollars and not exceeding five thousand dollars shall be paid one-half in cash at the time of sale, and a note or notes shall be given for the remaining half of the purchase price payable In three months with interest at the rate of five per centum per annum. Purchases over five thousand dollars and not exceeding ten thousand dollars shall be paid one-third in cash at the time of sale and notes shall be given for the remaining two-thirds of the purchase price, payable in three and six months, with interest at the rate of five per centum per annum. Purchases exceeding ten thousand dollars shall be paid one-fourth in cash at the time of sale and notes shall be given for the remaining three-fourths of the purchase price, payable in three, six and nine months with interest at the rate of five per centum per annum. Notes given as herein provided shall be made payable at a bank in the city or town in which the sale is held or at a bank in the city of Ottawa.
'So that, the department provides that in all cases under one thousand dollars the payment shall be in cash, and provides in every case for such payment as will enable the Department to receive the money before its security is gone. That meets the objection raised by my hon. friend.
Then why does the regulation say that the tender shall be accompanied by payment of the full amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that clause C reads:
No offer by tender shall be accepted unless accompanied by the full amount of the 'bonus.
Where it is sold by tender, that applies. Where it is sold by public auction, the regulations which I have just read apply. The practice is to sell entirely by public auction. This amendment leaves the mat- , ter just as it stood before in that respect, that wherever the sale is by tender the full amount must be paid.

In both cases it might be taken into consideration whether the principle might not be extended still further, so that the balance of the bonus unpaid might remain a charge on the remaining timber to be taken out. In that way the bonus would not be lost, because the money would be collected as the berth was being depreciated in value by the timber being taken out.
Is the uniform price of the license five dollars per mile?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: East of Yale the uniform price is five dollars per mile. West of Yale it is five cents per acre.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-conditions of licenses- erection of mills:
Mr.. BUREAU: In the case of an ordinary timber limit the purchaser has to erect a mill within a certain time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

It must have a capacity, I think, of a thousand feet a day for every two .and one half miles purchased, and it must be operated six months in the year. Is there any regulation, or any provision, that forces the purchaser of a pulpwood berth to erect a mill and operate it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have no provision up to the present time for selling the timber limits for the purpose of the pulpwood industry. This is our first venture in that line. We have already provided, in order to meet the new conditions, that no timber limit .shall be larger than twenty-five square miles. We here enact the clause that imposes on the pulpwood operator a corresponding obligation to that all along imposed on the lumber operator. But we have not had experience enough to enable us to say just exactly what character of mill that man should erect, and within what time, and so forth. Consequently, pending that provision, we place the power in the Bill to enable the minister to fix the nature of the mill to be erected, just as stated here.
Shall erect a mill or mills of such capacity and character, and at such point or points, and at such time or times, as the minister may decide.
Experience will teach us in this, as in the case of lumber mills, what should be required.

Has any discussion taken place with the officers of the department, or those who have been more especially charged with looking after the pulpwood berths, as to the conditions that will be imposed on the purchaser, the capacity of the mill, and the number of months it will have to be operated, or the quantity of wood the purchaser will have to saw a year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The form of regulations with respect to pulpwood has not yet been discussed with me. The officers of the department have the matter under consideration.
Will those regulations be published in the Official Gazette?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yee.
.Sir SAM HUGHES:	Has the minister
considered the point about the control of the limit. As. I understand the law, the minister has the option: of saying whether or not he will wipe that man out. In other words, the minister, or officers of the department, could close a man out by requiring him to put lip a mill of a certain size and under certain conditions, and operate it in a certain way, and could make it impossible for the owner to. carry on business. Why not fix it more definitely, and have a general clause in the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would be desirable
to fix it definitely, but we have not the data to enable us4o do it, and we do not think we are able to make all the provisions, at all events without some experience in the operation of the pu'lpwood industry.
I.s it the intention of the minister, before advertising a limit for sale, to set out the regulation as to the mill, and the cutting of the wood that would be necessary on that particular limit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

With reference to the amendment to section 15, I would like to ask why the minister is given discretionary powers as to the points at which mills have to be erected in connection with pulpwood concessions. At certain points along the Athabaska river where there are enormous areas of pulpwood, there is natural gas and at many places there are valuable water-powers. It might be more advantageous to the owner of a timber berth to erect his mill at a point where these natural resources could be made use of rather than at the point which the minister might designate. Therefore, I would ask why it should not be left to the owner to say where his mill should be located.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it is only proper that the department should have some say as to the location of the mill. It is quite true that no matter what power you put into the hands of the minister he may so exercise it as to be oppressive, but I think the principle is sound that the minister should have some supervision as to where the mills should be located in reference to the timber berth which he puts up for sale. Of course, the tenderers for that berth would be in a position to inquire as to what the requirements of the minister would be in

that regard; and so they would not be purchasing in the dark. This is similar to the regulations that have been in force for years in reference to lumbermen.
On section. 16-withdrawal of portion ol timber berths from license after notice:
Why ihas the notice been shortened from one year to sixty days?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The main purpose of the amendment is to enable withdrawals to be made for other useful purposes as well as for agricultural purposes. One year's notice has been given in the past, but the experience of the department is that a year is quite unnecessary and it is believed that sixty days is sufficient. When a year's notice is required it makes the regulation cf very little value.

It may not give a person sufficient time to remove camps or other things if only sixty days' notice is given. If it were in the summer season, or in the logging season, and the licensee were given notice to get out, it might mean that his license would be cancelled, his land withdrawn and be would not be in a position to take his property away.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In such case a longer time would be given- This is simply a minimum of sixty days, because in most cases sixty days is sufficient, but wherever more is in equity required, it is given.
On section 19-pulpwood included and area of tract extended;

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is to make a limit not exceeding one square mile -and it is to include pulpwood as well as timber and cordwood.
On section 22-no department employee to purchase land;
That is to prevent employees from dealing in land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. It means that an employee cannot get a homestead entry or deal in land in any way.
Does that prohibit an agent of the Government in the United States from dealing in land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

In the olden days Government land or immigration agents in the United States were privileged to take commissions on the sale of land, and I say advisedly that it was a very good1 plan. That was stopped and it had a very injur-
[Mr. Meighen.l
ions effect on immigration coming into our Northwest from the United States. I do not know whether this would 9 p.m. affect it or not. There is no reason why Government agents bringing in immigrants should not be authorized to sell land and -take a commission on it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It does not affect that point at all. The law as it stood forbade any employee of the Government to locate any land or act as agent for any other person in that behalf, and any employee violating that subsection was liable to dismissal. This amendment provides that an employee cannot take land by homesteading it or otherwise.
On section 2M-Cancel latkxn of letters patent or recommendation issued in error.
This is to allow the amendment of -the certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is all, on account of the certificate or recommendation.
On section 24-Cancellation of patent if issued through fraud, improvidence, ot in error.

Is there anything in the old Adt which authorizes -the department to take action similar to this?
Mr. MEIiQHEN:	Under the law as it
stands now, when the patent has once issued the only way -the department can have it cancelled is -by laying information in the Exchequer Court. That will still prevail, but additional provision i-s -made.

That is, after the patent has i-ssued?
Mr. (MEIGHEN: The Justice Department has held that as soon -as the patent is sealed it is issued, even though it remains in the department. Consequently, we cannot prevent the -man from getting the benefit of that patent, even though we find it has issued through fraud. The amendment enables us to cancel under such circumstances.

I do not want to get the reputation of being ia purist in language, but the -word " improvidence," I think, is intended to connote carelessness. I think what the law intends to convey is th-a-t the instrument has issued through fraud, or carelessness, ot error. " Improvidence " really -means extravagance, and I do not think that is what -is intended to be conveyed.
Mr. iMEIGHEN:	I think it is better to
retain the wording as it is, because in the

old Act exactly the same words are used: " WtheneveT letters patent, or other instrument respecting land have issued through fraud, or improvidence, or in error, any court having competent jurisdiction"-and so forth. When we aTe putting a proviso into the Act we had: better follow the same language. Doubtless there have been cases decided upon this provision, and I think the language should be continued.
I am not familiar with the wording of the old Act. Is the language here much the same as it is in the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The language is the
very same. We are using the old section just as it is, which enables1 us to go to the courts and secure cancellation of a patent issued through fraud, or improvidence, or in error; but it is provided in addition that if the patent had not left the department, even although legally issued at the time and with the seal of the Crown affixed the minister, upon proof of the improvidence, fraud or error, may himself cancel the patent without going to the court at all.

What strikes me is
that there may toe cases where the patentee may regard himself as being harshly treated if he has not got the right to appeal. In this case the minister seems to be the sole judge, andi no machinery is provided whereby the man interested has the opportunity of presenting his case. In connection with matters arising under other departments that opportunity is given. For instance, in the Department of Customs, if a vessel is seized for infraction of the customs laws, or improper entry, the minister may declare that the vessel be condemned, but the owner is given the opportunity of appeal within thirty days, either to the Government or to a court. Now I would like to see a loophole here for a man who feels himself aggrieved to present his case before some independent court, or to appeal to the 'Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The situation is this:
Up to the issue of a patent to a homesteader or a pre-emptor the minister is the judge as to whether or not he has earned that patent. There has never been any need for a court of appeal over the minister, although I presume that if a man Claimed to have lived up to all requirements of the law and then been' arbitrarily refused) his patent by the minister, he would be entitled to action against the Crown, andi he is entitled to that yet. But subject to that right, the minister has had1 the power of
decision as to whether or not the patent was coming to that man up to the moment of issue. After the issue then the minister could no longer decide, but if he wanted the patent cancelled he had to go to the court. All this amendment does is to extend that point very slightly. The minister has the power to decide not only up to the moment of the legal issue, which is the sealing of the patent with the seal of the Crown, but up to the moment that the patent leaves the department on its way to the patentee. I went into the matter with the Department of Justice and held that the patent was not issued at all until. it left the department. However, the Department of Justice took the view, and I think rightly, that the patent legally issues when the seal of the Crown is affixed. We therefore think that the minister's power should still be exercised, and should still prevail, up to. the -moment that the patent leaves the department.
On Section 25

Stock in lieu of cultivation in case of certain quarter-sections.
Will the minister indicate what changes, if any, have been made with reference to the substitution of cattle for the cultivation of the land?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Act says that the
holder of a pre-emption which is not of a class suitable for agriculture may substitute stock in lieu of cultivation, notwithstanding the fact that there may be a sufficient area of arable land on the homestead to allow the performance of cultivation, If the required area of arable land can be found either upon his- homestead or his pre-emption, the practice is to- require the entrant to do the necessary cultivation, and it is desired to bring the Act into conformity with the practice. That is the purpose of this amendment.
I would suggest that the minister use his discretion as to whether it is necessary for substantial buildings to be erected in certain localities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, where a
homesteader has his pre-emption as well, he may use the buildings now on the homestead. He may utilize those buildings wholly, and at the same time avail himself of the stock substitution regulation with regard to- his pre-emption; but it has never been felt that we could do away with the necessity of the buildings altogether and merely allow the homesteader to- put stock on the land. To do that would toe to invade, too seriously, I think, the spirit of the

regulation which requires the use of the land as a hamieet-ead for the purposes' of agriculture.
On section 26-Patent to be issued in name of deceased entrant in certain cases:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In British Columbia, while there is provision for the appointment of an administrator of the estate of a deceased person, no power is given to the administrator to acquire in his own name the real property of the deceased. Under the law as it stands now, therefore, there is imposed on the Department of the Interior, in relation to the Peace River land and the railway belt, the obligation of ascertaining who the heirs are. We think that is no part of our duty, and we are providing that in such cases the department, when the time comes to issue patents, may do so in the name of the deceased person. We do that now in the case of deceased soldiers, and we shall be doing it, if this Bill passes, in the case of patents of lands in British Columbia.
: No province, so far as I know, gives the administrator power so to acquire real estate.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The administrator has this power in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
At common law he would not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be his duty at common law simply to see that the estate was distributed to the heirs; but in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, where our Crown lands are, the administrator has power to take to himself the legal estate of the real property, and that enables us to convey to the administrator as soon as he is appointed any lands to which the deceased was entitled. We cannot do that in British Columbia; we are compelled to search out the heirs. We now wish to issue the patent simply in the name of the deceased and have the administrator distribute it according to the law of the province.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Before we come to the preamble I wish to submit an amendment which is to constitute section 27 of the Bill, the present section 27 to be section 28. The effect of the amendment is really to ratify the Order in Council, the spirit and purpose of which I stated to the House on moving the introduction of this Bill- 
to abolish altogether purchased homesteads and pre-emptions:
27. (1.) The privilege of pre-emption entry on Dominion lands as provided for by section 27 of the Dominion Lands Act, Chapter 20 of the Statutes of 1908, as amended hy sections 2 and 3 of chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1914, is hereby withdrawn.
(2.) The privileges of purchased homestead' entry as provided for by section 28 of ohapter 20 of the Statutes of 1908, as amended by section 4 of chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1914, is hereby withdrawn.
(3.) Where land has been reserved for preemption entry for any homesteader who is on active military service, or -where notice has been issued to any person allowing him a specified, time within which to appear and secure preemption or purchased homestead entry for a given quarter-section, such land may he sold to the homesteader or to the person so notified, at the rate of three dollar's per acre, subject to the duties, terms and conditions which would have obtained if the pre-emption and purchased homestead privilege had not been withdrawn.
(4.) This section shall be deemed to have come into operation on the twentieth day of March, 1918.
Why is the twentieth day of March particularly mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was the date the Order in Council was passed abolishing purchased homesteads and pre-emptions. It was considered wise to do it by Order in Council and subsequently to ratify it by legislation, for if we simply waited for the passing of the legislation there would likely be a rush for homesteads and pre-emptions, and to that extent the purpose of the amendment would have been defeated.
The old provision is in force only in respect of those who enlisted and are now at the front, and who made application for homestead before they left?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

It must have been a great relief to tlie broad-minded, nonpartisan Minister of the Interior when patronage was abolished in all departments, for I am sure that it would grate upon his nerves and feelings if he had to divide the population into two camps and be kind to some and do nothing for others. But something is still lingering behind which looks like patronage, and it is found in the different Tory newspapers in my part of the country. In the Sydney Post, for instance, which I have before me, I find a synopsis of the coal mining regulations, to which is appended the name of the Deputy Minister of the Interior. This notice finds its way into all the Tory papers of Nova Scotia, but by no chance gets into others. If patron-

age is abolished the minister should eliminate this patronage altogether, or, if such advertising is necessary in his department, give a share of it to the Grit papers, which are, if anything, more widely read in Nova Scotia than the Tory publications.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend's principles are sound, but his information is rather antiquated. Patronage is abolished wholly. The advertisement my hon. friend refers to is, I assume, from a paper of last month, because while it was possible for us to abolish patronage, we could not regard existing contracts as " scraps of paper."
Mr. McKENZilE: The date of this paper is March 22.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These contracts are contracts, and all of them expired, I think, at the end of March; but after the expiry of these contracts, these regulations are no longer inserted in any paper, Unionist, Liberal, or Conservative, and thereby the country is saved a very large annual outlay.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On the preamble:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall not ask that we carry the preamble. I wish to leave the Bill in Committee for this reason: I have under consideration an amendment which I purpose submitting, providing for a change in the law relating to the interest on school land sales. The amendment will be ready when the House next goes into Committee. I, therefore, move: That the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Will the minister tell us the purport of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I speak what is now in my mind in this regard. It is this, that as to all future sales the rate of interest shall be raised from 5 per cent to 6 per cent with 7 per cent on arrears. That is to say; suppose that the terms are one-tenth down and the balance one-tenth yearly for nine successive payments with interest at six per cent; then if a purchaser permits his payments, whether of interest or of principal, to run into arrears, he shall pay seven pear cent on those arrears. As regard past sales, a difficulty arises, because they have been made on express terms, and, of course, in so far as a purchaser lives up to those terms, his contract will not be interfered with; but where a purchaser fails to live up to those terms, the department has not power to raise the rate of interest without his consent, and it is proposed to ask for
power, on obtaining his consent, to raise the rate of interest on arrears to seven per cent in respect of those sales as well. We are, of course, able to obtain his consent unless he is prepared to pay up the arrears, because the power of cancellation is vested in Council.
It will not be a hold-up?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The idea is that as regards arrears the rate of interest shall hereafter (be seven per cent, and that in new sales the rate of interest on money not in arrears shall be six per cent. The idea is to make it in the interest of purchasers to pay up in accordance with their contracts and not merely to hold school land for purposes of speculation and not even pay interest or principal.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This Bill is to confirm an agreement for the leasing of a stretch of about two miles of the Bangor and Aroostook railway between the International and Transcontinental railways. The Bangor and Aroostook railway runs from the state of Maine across the Transcontinental and up to the International, and our object in

leasing this line is to do away with the upkeep of two stations. When this agreement is ratified, the trains now going over the International will go over these two miles of line, and the Transcontinental station at St. Leonard' will serve as a union station for both lines. We shall then require -but one set of station -agents and shall save the operating expenses on two miles of road. The lease exipires in 1934, which is the year when the bonds of this railway fall due. The owners could not sell this railway or we would have purchased it. The rental is $1,200 a year, which is the estimated amount of the interest on this portion of the railway. At the expiration of the lease the Government will have to consider whether to take a further lease or purchase the two miles.

I have just arrived from home where I had -an opportunity of interviewing the residents of the village of St-. Leonard, and I have here a petition, also a number of letters and telegrams, protesting against the leasing of this road, if it be the Government's intention to have a union station for the International and Transcontinental.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Our object in acquiring this piece of road is to have a union station for the International and the Transcontinental. At present passengers coming in on the International have to drive.or walk over the Transcontinental if they are going on to Levis or Moncton. The union station will obviate that.

It is all very well for the minister to say that if passengers on the International want to go to Quebec or Moncton they have to walk or drive over to the Transcontinental railway station, but as a matter of fact the Transcontinental train passes through St. Leonard, going west, at three o'clock in the morning, and . going east, at twelve midnight; so hardly any one travels over that road because of the inconvenient hours. On the other hand, it is very easy for them to catch the Canadian Pacific, which runs parallel to the Transcontinental. The people of St. Leonard object very strongly to the idea of this union station. It is proposed to be built outside of the village altogether, about a quarter to half a mile away. With your permission, Mi-. Chairman, I shall read the following petition without reciting all the names, prepared by the citizens of St. Leonard against this proposed legislation:

To the Honourable Minister of Railways and Canals of Canada, Ottawa, Canada.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: THE HUMBLE PETITION OF THE CITIZENS OF THE VILLAGE OF ST. LEONARD, IN THE COUNTY OF MADAWASKA,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AND PROVINCE OF NEW BRUNSWICK HUMBLY SHEWETH:
That we the undersigned citizens and residents of the Village of St. Leonard, N. B., are desirous that the terminus of the International railway shall remain at its present location and are all strongly opposed- to the erection of a Union Station at or near the St. Leonard Station of the National Transcontinental railway for the following reasons:
1.	That the present location of the terminus and station of the International railway is to the best advantage to all the citizens of the said village, and to the best accommodation to all the travelling public;
2.	That there is no local train service on the National Transcontinental railway of any kind for passengers nor other local accommodation. The only passenger trains are the one north-bound due at St. Leonard, N. B., at 12 p.m. and the south-bound at 3 a.m., thereby no train service at the dispositions of the local travelling public;
3.	That passengers from the International Railway points desirous to make connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway trains for local points, as well as passengers from other points to points on the International railway, would be compelled to travel for a 10 minutes' walk or in cab, the baggage to be transferred by truck teams, if the proposed union station is built at the Transcontinental railway, to the great disadvantage of all the passengers as well as the citizens of our village. Furthermore that it will be removing local train accommodation from the most business centre of our village to a location most out of the way for all the people's advantage, except a very few families in that direction.
4.	That such ohange in the terminus of the International railway and its passenger station and freight office will lead -beyond any doubt to the detriment of the future as well as of the present welfare of our village and its citizens.
And further pray that this our petition be approved as to the views and opinions of the undersigned, and that instead of a Union Station being built at the Transcontinental railway as proposed, a passenger station be built at or near the place of -the present terminus and yard of the International railway at or about the most business centre of our village.
We therefore humbly pray and urge for your serious consideration the urgent need- of granting our request.
As in duty bound we will ever pray.
This is signed by all the merchants of the village of St. Leonard. I think there are between 70 and 100 signatures, including members of the legal -profession, customs officers, postmasters, station agents and men of other professions. I have no doubt the hon. minister wants to do what is right by the people of St. Leonard. I have visited the place where the station is proposed to be (built, and I have also seen where the

old station in connection with the International railway was huilt. You are doing a great harm to the people of St. Leonard if you remove the present station of the International railway and build a union station outside the town altogether. While they were trying to get an Act passed in this House to build that short line of railway, to unite the Van Buren bridge with the International railway, the citizens of St. Leonard objected strongly to that short line of railway, for the reason that the Americans were building a bridge over the St. John river in order to connect with the International railway, for one purpose only, namely, to be able to transport our national resources in the province of iNe-w Brunswick into the state of Maine. They have been transporting our national resources, pulp-wood deals, manufactured lumber, and other kinds of wood. When the Act was about to be passed in this House I received a message from the citizens of St. Leonard asking, before the Act be passed, that a certain provision be inserted. I could not obtain the Act to-night, but I will produce it at the next sitting of the House. The telegram was as .follows:
Give your hearty support for railway bridge here providing that it is strictly understood thajt International station and terminus remain in St. Leonard Village at its present location.
That is where the station of the International railway is now built. They ask that it shall remain whore it is. I do not think the minister will desire to remove it at the present moment unless he wants to change the whole line. That telegram is signed by five citizens of St. Leonard.

speechtext: Do I understand that is the charter that was got by the Van Buren Bridge Company, or by the International Railway Company?

speechtext:
I believe it was the Van Buren Bridge Company, and they are the people who built up the short line of railway which you are about to lease under this Act. If you are going to lease that short line of railway, and remove the railway station, because you are buying that short line of railway, you are not following the provisions of the Bill. The Bill says you cannot remove the station except to the International railway, and that the terminus shall remain at St. Leonard in its present location. From my point of view, it would be unfair now to change the whole law. I have been asked to state by whom this message was signed. I find the following signatures: F. C. Rivard, J. R. Cyr,
B. R. Violette, Raymond Hebert, A. J. Violette. These are the leading men of the village of St. Leonard. I would ask the hon. minister to give me an opportunity at the next sitting of the House to produce the Bill passed in 1913, wherein we can find .a clause providing that the. terminus of the International railway and its station cannot be changed from one place to another. ,1 hope he will give me an opportunity at the next session of the House to produce the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: THE HUMBLE PETITION OF THE CITIZENS OF THE VILLAGE OF ST. LEONARD, IN THE COUNTY OF MADAWASKA,
speechtext: Of course, the hon. gentleman knows the locality better than I do. I have never been in St. Leonard, and I have simply to take the statement of the officials of the road. As I understand the situation, there are now three railway stations in St. Leonard, the National Transcontinental station on the through line between Levis and Moncton, the Canadian Pacific Railway station on the line that runs through St. Leonard, and the station of the International railway. The Government owning both the International and the Transcontinental and keeping up two sets of employees at the two stations, I think the House will agree with me that that is hardly fair or right. The proposal is that the International railway shall have its terminal at the Transcontinental station. If this is not done, we must keep up the two stations. You may change the location of the station on the International, but you must maintain the station on the main line (between Levis and Moncton. When the matter was brought to my attention by the officials of the department it struck me as a reasonable business proposition and one to which I could not see that any person could object. The hon. gentleman raises objections, one of them being that the trains go through on the Transcontinental road, that there are no local trains and therefore, it would not be of service. I can hardly see that is a reason why the trains should not have their terminus at the same station. I do not see why you should keep the 'International station where it is because it is a little nearer the Canadian Pacific. The hon. gentleman has raised two questions which of course I shall look into. One is that the station on the Transcontinental is not proposed to be placed in as convenient a spot for the public. If the Transcontinental had their station built there, and all completed, it would be rather difficult to move it now. I do not see how I could agree to that, without looking further into It. The bon. gentleman also

The minister has appointed! quite a number of inspectors; or perhaps they were appointed before the minister took charge of the department. I understand their duties to be
10 p.m. connected with the inspection of salted and pickled herring. Some years ago oyster culture was carried on in the waters of Prince Edward Island. I am sorry to say that the succulent Malpeque is fast disappearing, and the same fate appears to be overtaking the oysters at Miscou, New Brunswick. I think it would be in the interest of consumers if the department would, under the diligent and energetic direction of my hon. friend (Mr. Ballan-tyne) look carefully after this food. The Malpeque oyster is, as the minister knows, a very excellent food, and commands the respect of aJll the connoisseurs in North America. It is really a pity to see the excellent Malpeque oyster disappearing so rapidly. I remember that some years ago an effort was made by the department to promote oyster culture, but I do not know what progress has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The private oyster beds have been taken over by the several provincial governments, therefore, oyster culture is now in the hands of the provincial authorities.

I want to ask a question or two of the minister, and at the same time to congratulate him upon the resolution he has made in regard to the carrying on of the business of the department. I have had occasion during the last two or three years to draw the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, whilst the estimates were under discussion, to a situation which prevailed in the province from which I come in regard to the inspectors, fishery overseers and wardens, and I have never yet been able to get an absolute answer as regards these different classes of officers. Now, there is a multiplicity of officers along all the sea coasts of Canada who pretend to look after the fishing rights and interests in their respective localities. I find on pages R 46 and 47 of the Auditor General's Report for the year ending 31st of March, 1917, reference made to the fishery overseers and inspectors in the province of New Brunswick. Did I understand the minister to say that the term of office of the overseers and wardens expired on the 31st of March last?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, what I said was that the term of office of the wardens, who are also known as guardians, did expire on the 31st of March, hut not so with the overseers or the fishery inspectors, who are permanent.

I have noticed that there are inspectors, overseers and wardens, and also special guardians. In the province of New Brunswick, I notice, the special guardians during the year ending 31st of Alarch, 1917, cost $33,933.85- Am I to understand that these officers have been abolished, and that there are no special guardians in existence to-day ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

So much with respeot to that. I have on previous occasions drawn the attention of ithe department to what I believe to be an absolutely irregular, unnecessary, and unbusinesslike way of engaging and paying the overseers and wardens. It is a different matter with the inspectors. There is a certain number of these officials who have prescribed areas over which they exercise control.
There are a number of inspectors, each in charge of a zone or area and each in receipt of a fairly good salary. One of the inspectors in New Brunswick gets $2,000, besides travelling expenses, $787; allowance for stenographer, and so on. The overseers and wrardens are also paid salaries. For instance, Mr. Prescott, of Baie Verte, gets the magnificent salary of $150 a year, but for travelling outlay he received last year $752.70. I know the location; I know what has taken place in that office during the last number of years. These men are paid practically no salary, but they send in a report as to mileage and that is the way they make up their salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They cannot live on $150.

No, they cannot live on that amount. In the same locality there is an inspector at Barachois, Mr. Vinneau, whose salary is only $120 a year. He does the same work as Mr. Prescott, but strange to say his travelling outlay last year was $1,022.30. This is an indication of what has been taking place in the department for some years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These guardians are allowed ten cents a mile when they travel. Apparently these two men have done considerable travelling; I have no way of checking that up just now.

The department should have some check on these matters. They should pay these men a reasonable salary and require them to make proper returns and give full value for what they receive, or be subject to dismissal. What is true of these two cases is true of the other overseers and wardens. I hope the minister will see that his department is placed on a business basis and operated along business lines, irrespective of political favours.
I wish also to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that was referred to in the House early last session. Along the shores of New Brunswick, not far from my own county, illegal lobster fishing has been

going on. The inspector sent his patrol boat out, caught the men fishing lobsters out of season, seized the boats, and, I think destroyed one. When it was found that boats belonged to some person friendly to the Government, close to the department, a commissioner was appointed to investigate the matter, and I have a copy of the return that was brought down containing all the evidence. I notice that an amount for legal expenses is charged up in connection with this investigation. If the minister will look at the commissioner's report he may readily draw a conclusion whether there was illegal lobster fishing in this case and whether the person whose boats were seized was properly dealt with toy the inspector. The inspector tried to do his work in a proper manner, but as soon as it interfered with some who had pull, the inspector's jurisdiction was set aside, the matter taken out of his hands and a commissioner appointed to investigate. I draw the minister's attention to these facts simply to point out to him that he has a great gulf or chasm to bridge in order to get away from what has been going on in his department during the last few years.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the explanation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with reference to this item. I am pleased, indeed, to hear that he is going to make a change in the appointment of fishery guardians. The minister should toe congratulated that at last he has taken hold of this part of his department in a tousinesslike manner. The county from which I come is, perhaps, the largest fishing county in Canada-and I have in mind other counties in Nova Scotia where these guardians have been appointed during the last twenty years and where there was really no necessity for them at all. I suggest that great care toe exercised with reference to those who appoint these guardians. I think the minister said that the appointments were to be made toy the Civil Service Commission.,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The appointments are in the hands of the Civil Service Commission, tout if that body needs any advice -and I assume it will-the inspector of the district in question would toe the man from whom we should seek advice. If we find that he is not giving us the kind of advice that we would expect to get from a business man then we will put another inspector in charge of that district.

I conclude my remarks to the minister toy merely saying that the House

would like him to give instructions to those inspectors to toe sure to -employ men who are not partisans, but who will do their duty.

In regard to the minister's explanation as to the decrease of $101,000, I understand that the decrease in the number of overseers will account for some portion of it, but I would like to know what portion of the decrease is accounted for by the decrease in the staff and what portion by the decrease in other expenses.
Mr. BAXiLANTYlNE : I do not agree with the cut in the estimates of $101,000 that has been made here, and I think I shall be forced a little later on to insert it in my supplementary estimates. Mr. McMAiS'TER: We were going to congratulate the minister on the decrease.
